01
What Drives Amazon’s Revenue? Category, Product and Location Analysis (2025)

This analysis investigates which products, categories and locations drive revenue, by running SQL summary statistics and group breakdowns on 250 Amazon orders. The analysis shows Electronics as the strongest category, Refrigerators and Laptops dominating revenue, Houston, Seattle and Miami as top locations (excluding cancelled orders) and PayPal as the leading payment method.

Recommendations: prioritise inventory on the top products, tune regional pricing, and optimise payment channels to maximise revenue.

Languages, tools and platforms: PostgreSQL, Tableau
Analysis: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), Descriptive Statistics, Geospatial Analysis, Performance Analysis, Time Series Analysis

Details & datasets Tableau dashboard
02
What Are the Leading Causes of Death in England and Wales? Mortality Analysis (2025)

Drawing on the Office for National Statistics’ mortality data released in September 2026, this dashboard looks at the leading causes of death in England and Wales in 2025, covering 570,988 deaths (534,020 in England, 35,767 in Wales and 1,201 non-residents). The results show dementia and Alzheimer's as the leading cause at 72,272 deaths, ahead of ischaemic heart diseases at 52,639, with dementia claiming more women (45,874 vs 26,398 men) and ischaemic heart disease more men (35,481 vs 17,158 women). The mean age at death is 81 for women and 77 for men.

Over the decade from 2016 to 2025, annual deaths peaked at around 605,000 in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic before settling at roughly 568,000 in 2025, while among injury-related causes, intracranial injury (4,669), asphyxiation (3,691) and fracture of the femur (3,455) lead.

Languages, tools and platforms: PostgreSQL, DBeaver, Tableau
Analysis: Exploratory Data Analysis, Demographic Analysis, Time Series Analysis

Details & datasets Tableau dashboard
03
Superstore Sales vs Profit Analysis: Where Does the Business Make and Lose Money?

This dashboard explores how profitability varies across regions, customer segments and product categories, built from 9,994 superstore records. The results show £2.3M in sales and £286k in profit at a 12.5% profit ratio, with most states profitable but Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Tennessee and Colorado showing weaker or negative profit ratios, and sales across all segments and categories peaking towards the end of 2021.

Filtering by region, order date and profit ratio helps stakeholders find high-margin segments and geographic expansion opportunities.

Languages, tools and platforms: Tableau
Analysis: Profitability Analysis, Segmentation Analysis, Geospatial Analysis, Time Series Analysis

Details & dataset Tableau dashboard
04
What Influences a Diabetes Diagnosis? Risk Factor Analysis of 700,000 Patients

Which factors raise the odds of a diabetes diagnosis? This project examines which health, lifestyle and demographic factors drive a diagnosis, built from 700,000 patient records and 24 variables. The results show family history as the strongest driver, with 86.7% of patients with a family history diagnosed versus 58.0% without, followed by age, where diagnosis rises from 42.5% in 18-30s to 68.1% in over-50s, and then blood pressure, BMI and cholesterol. Physical activity is the main protective factor, while smoking status, employment and sleep hours show almost no difference between groups.

Languages, tools and platforms: PostgreSQL, Tableau
Analysis: Spread Analysis, Risk Segmentation, Correlation Analysis, Demographic Analysis

Details & datasets Tableau dashboard
05
From CoinGecko to PostgreSQL: Automating Daily Cryptocurrency Data with an ETL Pipeline

Automated a pipeline using Python and PostgreSQL, scheduled by cron, that fetches live cryptocurrency prices from CoinGecko and cleans the data automatically, delivering validated, formatted cryptocurrency data without manual intervention. The SQL stored procedure handles deduplication, null value management, and data standardization every morning at 6:05 AM, eliminating 30 minutes of daily manual work while ensuring consistency and reliability.

Languages, tools and platforms: Python, PostgreSQL, Cron
Analysis: Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) Pipeline

Details & code
06
From 136 Messy Rows to 79 Clean Records: Cleaning Student Data with PostgreSQL

Sourced a 136-row student records dataset with a tangled mix of pipe delimiters, missing names, currency confusion, duplicate entries, truncated and misspelled course names, and dates formatted inconsistently. Using PostgreSQL in DBeaver, I built a systematic multi-stage pipeline: extracting data from malformed fields, standardising dates and currencies, identifying and removing duplicates, and handling problematic enrollment dates and missing values. The result: 79 clean, usable records ready for analysis.

Languages, tools and platforms: PostgreSQL, DBeaver
Analysis: Data Cleaning

Case study

Student records data cleaning

The raw export mixed pipe-delimited and comma-delimited rows in the same file, with trailing commas, "NA" and NULL placeholders, truncated course names, and a batch of rows that had been pasted in twice. In PostgreSQL, SPLIT_PART() extracted the real fields from those malformed rows. CASE statements then converted placeholder values into proper NULLs. A ROW_NUMBER() window function identified duplicates for removal. String functions repaired truncated and misspelled course names as part of handling data quality issues. Type conversions standardised dates across inconsistent formats—some ISO, some DD-MM-YY—and unified three different currency symbols into GBP. The cleaned records were saved to a view for consistent formatting and easy querying. Each step was validated against the source data to catch edge cases.

Data Analysis Project

Amazon Sales Data Analysis

I carried out this analysis in PostgreSQL, using DBeaver as the platform, on 250 Amazon orders, in two stages. First, a summary statistics script profiled the three numeric fields (price, quantity and total sales) using ten measures each: count, sum, mean, standard deviation, mode, minimum, quartiles, median and maximum. This set a baseline for how orders are distributed before any comparisons were made. Second, a group statistics script broke the data down across five categorical columns (category, product, customer location, payment method and order status), calculating average price, average quantity, total quantity, average sales and total sales for every group. The results were then visualised in an interactive Tableau dashboard, and both SQL scripts and all datasets are available below.

Data Visualization Project

Mortality in England and Wales, 2025

My Process: I sourced this data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), using the mortality data for England and Wales released in September 2026. I carried out exploratory data analysis on the dataset in PostgreSQL using DBeaver, writing queries to shape it into the breakdowns the dashboard needed, such as leading causes of death, deaths by sex, injury-related causes and yearly totals. I then exported the results as custom files and imported them into Tableau to build the visualisation.
Dashboard Question Answered: What are the leading causes of death in England and Wales, how do they differ between women and men, and how have total deaths changed over the last decade?

This interactive Tableau dashboard opens with headline figures for 2025: 534,020 deaths in England, 35,767 in Wales and 1,201 among non-residents, split into 279,624 female and 291,364 male deaths, with a mean age at death of 81 for women and 77 for men. A ranked chart shows dementia and Alzheimer's as the leading cause (72,272 deaths), followed by ischaemic heart diseases (52,639), chronic lower respiratory diseases, cerebrovascular diseases, lung and bronchus cancer, and influenza and pneumonia. A female vs male comparison reveals that dementia affects women far more (45,874 vs 26,398), while ischaemic heart disease affects men far more (35,481 vs 17,158). A ten-year line chart shows annual deaths rising from around 522,000 in 2016 to a peak in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, then settling at roughly 568,000 in 2025, and a treemap breaks down the top injury-related causes of death.

Data Visualization Project

Factors Influencing Diabetes Diagnosis

Dashboard Question Answered: How do health, lifestyle and demographic factors combine to create high-risk profiles for a diabetes diagnosis?

This interactive Tableau dashboard is built from two sources: the dataset itself, and a PostgreSQL spread analysis that I wrote first to guide it. The spread analysis bands each variable into categories (for example low, moderate and high BMI) and measures the gap between the highest and lowest diagnosis rate within each one. That ranking shaped which factors the dashboard features, alongside the analysis done directly on the dataset in Tableau. A risk-profile heatmap shows diagnosis rates for combinations of the factors that had the highest impact on a diabetes diagnosis: BMI, age, systolic blood pressure, LDL and total cholesterol, and family history. A correlation chart ranks each feature against diagnosis, and a demographic selector shows diagnosis rates and group sizes side by side. Across the dataset, 62.3% of patients have a diagnosis.
700,000 Records Analysed
24 Variables Compared
62.3% Diagnosed Diabetes
Key Features
SQL Spread Analysis
Banded 24 variables into categories in PostgreSQL and ranked each by the gap between its highest and lowest diagnosis rate, to decide which factors deserved space on the dashboard.
Combined Risk Heatmap
Each cell is one combination of BMI, age, systolic blood pressure, LDL, total cholesterol and family history risk levels. Colour shows the average diagnosis rate, and hover tooltips reveal the full profile.
Feature Correlation
Ranks each feature's correlation with diagnosis. Family history (0.21) and age (0.16) lead, while physical activity (−0.17) is the strongest protective factor.
Risk Spread Within Factors
Bar chart of diagnosis-rate spread for every factor. For each factor I created groups within its column where none existed, then compared diagnosis rates as patients move from one group to the next to see whether risk rises or falls, for example whether the risk of diabetes increases as people move into older age groups.
Demographic Selector
A parameter control switches between demographics such as age group, showing diagnosis rates and group sizes together so small groups are not over-read.

Automation Project

From CoinGecko to PostgreSQL: Automating Daily Cryptocurrency Data with an ETL Pipeline

A fully automated end-to-end ETL pipeline that runs every morning at 6:00 AM and 6:05 AM. The Python script fetches live cryptocurrency prices for 10 major coins (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether, Binance Coin, USD Coin, Ripple, Cardano, Solana, Tron, Polkadot) from the CoinGecko API, capturing price, market cap, and 24-hour trading volume. The raw data is inserted into PostgreSQL's crypto_raw table. Five minutes later, a SQL stored procedure automatically cleans and standardizes the data: converting coin names to uppercase, rounding prices to 8 decimals, handling null values with COALESCE, filtering duplicates to keep only the most recent price per coin, and validating data integrity. The cleaned dataset is populated into crypto_clean, eliminating manual intervention entirely and ensuring consistent, error-free data ready for daily analysis.

10cryptocurrencies tracked
3data points per coin

Python Script: fetch_crypto_data.py
import requests import psycopg2 from datetime import datetime def fetch_crypto_data(): """ Fetch cryptocurrency data from CoinGecko API """ print("🔄 Fetching cryptocurrency data from CoinGecko API...") url = "https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/simple/price" params = { 'ids': 'bitcoin,ethereum,tether,binancecoin,usd-coin,ripple,cardano,solana,tron,polkadot', 'vs_currencies': 'usd', 'include_market_cap': 'true', 'include_24hr_vol': 'true' } try: response = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print(f"✅ Successfully fetched data for: {list(data.keys())}") return data except Exception as e: print(f"❌ Error fetching data: {e}") return None def insert_raw_data(data): """ Connect to PostgreSQL and insert raw cryptocurrency data """ if not data: print("❌ No data to insert") return try: conn = psycopg2.connect( host="localhost", database="postgres", user="postgres", password="0989!!" ) cursor = conn.cursor() print("💾 Inserting data into PostgreSQL...") for coin, prices in data.items(): cursor.execute( """ INSERT INTO crypto_raw (coin_name, price, market_cap, volume) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s) """, ( coin, prices.get('usd'), prices.get('usd_market_cap'), prices.get('usd_24h_vol') ) ) conn.commit() print(f"✅ Successfully inserted {len(data)} coins into crypto_raw") cursor.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM crypto_raw") total_records = cursor.fetchone()[0] print(f"📊 Total records in crypto_raw: {total_records}") cursor.close() conn.close() except Exception as e: print(f"❌ Database error: {e}") if __name__ == "__main__": print("=" * 50) print("CRYPTOCURRENCY DATA AUTOMATION") print(f"Started at: {datetime.now()}") print("=" * 50) crypto_data = fetch_crypto_data() if crypto_data: insert_raw_data(crypto_data) print("=" * 50) print(f"Completed at: {datetime.now()}") print("=" * 50)
SQL Stored Procedure: clean_cryptocurrency_data()
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE clean_cryptocurrency_data() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE v_records_cleaned INT; BEGIN RAISE NOTICE '===================================='; RAISE NOTICE 'Starting cryptocurrency data cleaning'; RAISE NOTICE 'Time: %', NOW(); RAISE NOTICE '===================================='; DELETE FROM crypto_clean; INSERT INTO crypto_clean (coin_name, price_usd, market_cap_usd, volume_usd) SELECT UPPER(coin_name) as coin_name, ROUND(price, 8) as price_usd, COALESCE(market_cap, 0) as market_cap_usd, COALESCE(volume, 0) as volume_usd FROM crypto_raw WHERE (coin_name, fetched_at) IN ( SELECT coin_name, MAX(fetched_at) FROM crypto_raw GROUP BY coin_name ) AND price IS NOT NULL AND coin_name IS NOT NULL AND price > 0; GET DIAGNOSTICS v_records_cleaned = ROW_COUNT; RAISE NOTICE '===================================='; RAISE NOTICE 'Cleaning completed successfully!'; RAISE NOTICE 'Records cleaned: %', v_records_cleaned; RAISE NOTICE 'Time: %', NOW(); RAISE NOTICE '===================================='; END; $$; call clean_cryptocurrency_data(); select * from crypto_clean select '===RAW DATA==' as section; SELECT * FROM crypto_raw ORDER BY fetched_at; SELECT '=== CLEAN DATA ===' as section; SELECT * FROM crypto_clean;
